open_points.subject: credential file decoding
open_points.text: “its content decoded as UTF-8, without one trailing newline, is the value” and “holds an empty value or a control character”
open_points.question: What exactly counts as the removable trailing newline and as a forbidden control character?
options: Remove one LF only; reject any remaining Unicode control character
Remove one LF or CRLF; reject ASCII C0, DEL and C1 controls
Remove all trailing line endings before validating
open_points.default_guess: Remove exactly one final LF, treating a preceding CR as a forbidden control character, and reject ASCII C0, DEL and C1 controls.

open_points.subject: credential HTTP header value
open_points.text: “A resolved value is added as that header.”
open_points.question: Which decoded credential values are legal HTTP header values, and how are non-ASCII characters encoded on the wire?
options: Require visible ASCII plus permitted horizontal space
Permit HTTP Latin-1 field values
Encode the UTF-8 text as UTF-8 header bytes
open_points.default_guess: Require a nonempty visible-ASCII value with no leading or trailing whitespace and refuse anything else as credential_unresolved.

open_points.subject: selected service instance
open_points.text: “the selected manifest instance name of each service it selects one for” and “A service with no selected instance is not invocable”
open_points.question: What happens when configuration names an instance that does not exist in the configured manifest revision?
options: Refuse kernel startup
Treat the service as having no selected instance
Treat it as an instance with a missing address
open_points.default_guess: Refuse kernel startup because the installation selection is invalid.

open_points.subject: configuration token re-read
open_points.text: A17 requires the configuration file to be a regular, non-symbolic-link, owner-only file, while A16 says “Exactly four checks apply to a re-read” and lists only parsing and token-list checks.
open_points.question: After startup, must every token-list re-read repeat A17's secure-open, ownership, type and permission checks, or may it accept tokens from a file that would fail A17 at startup?
options: Repeat all A17 file-security checks on every re-read
Apply only A16's four checks after startup
Stop the kernel if the file-security properties changed
open_points.default_guess: Securely open the file and repeat A17's file-security checks on every re-read; refuse requests until they pass.

open_points.subject: owner and agent token secrecy
open_points.text: State 0 says “service credentials and tokens live in the installation's protected configuration; the kernel never puts one into a function, a flow, a trace or an answer,” but A17's concrete non-disclosure rules cover only service credential values.
open_points.question: What exact storage, tracing, failure-detail and logging prohibitions apply to the owner and agent tokens received with requests?
options: Apply the same no-store/no-trace/no-log/no-response rule as service credentials
Forbid them only in responses and records
Rely on the MCP host to prevent token logging
open_points.default_guess: Apply the full credential non-disclosure rule to owner and agent token values, including logs and failure details.

open_points.subject: data-directory privacy
open_points.text: “The directory and everything in it are private to the kernel's user; the kernel refuses to start otherwise.”
open_points.question: Which ownership and permission bits constitute “private,” and must the rule be checked recursively for directories as well as regular files?
options: Every entry must be owned by the kernel user and grant no group/other permissions
Only the data-directory root must be owner-only
Directories may grant execute permission to group or others but files may not
open_points.default_guess: Require the root and every existing descendant to be owned by the kernel user with no group or other permission bits.

open_points.subject: missing data directory
open_points.text: “At start it takes an exclusive lock in the data directory” and “The data directory holds one SQLite database…”
open_points.question: If the configured data directory or its required subdirectories/database do not exist, does the kernel create them or refuse to start?
options: Create the directory and initial store with private permissions
Require the directory but create internal store files
Require the complete store layout and refuse otherwise
open_points.default_guess: Create a missing data directory and store layout with owner-only permissions, but refuse an existing invalid layout.

open_points.subject: symbolic link encountered during a store call
open_points.text: Rule 2 says a later symbolic link “makes that store call fail with nothing written,” while rule 3 says a failed call may leave “a published file no record names.”
open_points.question: May a store call that later encounters a symbolic link leave files it published earlier in that call, or must it roll them back so literally nothing was written?
options: No database records may remain, but unnamed published files may remain
Neither records nor published files may remain
The answer depends on whether publication preceded the symbolic-link check
open_points.default_guess: Leave no records but permit complete unnamed published files, which startup cleanup removes.

open_points.subject: scope of symbolic-link checks
open_points.text: “Every file of the directory is opened without following symbolic links; a link found at start stops the start” and the invariant “symlink_inside(data_directory) -> refused.”
open_points.question: Does the prohibition include symbolic links used as directories, the data-directory path itself, SQLite sidecar files and every recursively nested entry?
options: Reject any symbolic link at or below the data-directory path
Reject only links in the value, fixture and spool areas
Reject only a link encountered when opening a file
open_points.default_guess: Reject any symbolic link in the data-directory path or anywhere recursively beneath it.

open_points.subject: startup cleanup failures
open_points.text: “On start, temporary files, value bytes no record names … and the spool directories … are removed”; only failure to remove an obsolete spool directory is explicitly said not to stop startup.
open_points.question: What happens if startup cannot remove a temporary file or an unreferenced value byte?
options: Refuse startup
Continue but never serve the leftover object
Continue and retry removal on a later start
open_points.default_guess: Refuse startup for temporary or unreferenced value-area cleanup failures; retain the explicit continue behavior only for obsolete spool directories.

open_points.subject: store record order
open_points.text: “Activation M09 and FlowActivation M18 records are identified by their position in the store's one order of records” and “one writer … so records have one order.”
open_points.question: How is the position assigned when one transaction creates several records, and does updating an entity's status change its position?
options: Assign monotonically increasing positions in an explicitly defined insertion order; updates retain the original position
Give every mutation a new position
Use SQLite row order or transaction commit order implicitly
open_points.default_guess: Assign a monotonic position to each newly created record in the order the store call lists its writes; later updates retain that position.

open_points.subject: record and content-file crash consistency
open_points.text: “a completed file a record names is never overwritten” and failed calls may leave only an unnamed published file
open_points.question: What ordering and recovery rule guarantees that a committed record can never name a file that was not durably published when a crash occurs between file publication and the SQLite commit?
options: Durably publish and verify all files before committing their records
Commit records first and repair missing files at startup
Use an explicit journal spanning files and SQLite
open_points.default_guess: Durably publish and verify every referenced file before committing the transaction; a crash may therefore create only unreferenced files.

open_points.subject: retrying a waiting mapped element
open_points.text: A13 says a mapped node runs elements that have “no concluded record” and that “a concluded element is never executed again,” while A14 and A11 require new attempts after service_unreachable and after an unknown attempt is resolved not_applied, even though those elements already have NodeExecution records.
open_points.question: Does “concluded record” mean any NodeExecution, or only a record whose derived element conclusion is final, and how is a waiting element selected for its next attempt?
options: Only a final derived element conclusion prevents another attempt
Any NodeExecution prevents another attempt
Retries use a separate scheduling path outside A13's mapped-node rule
open_points.default_guess: Only a final derived element conclusion prevents another attempt; waiting records do not prevent a later numbered attempt.

open_points.subject: service_unreachable and outcome_unknown conclusions
open_points.text: A13 says “service_unreachable and outcome_unknown are waits … until the owner's resolution makes the element count as succeeded or failed,” but service_unreachable is retried by an owner or agent resume, and resolving outcome_unknown as not_applied makes the element wait for approval rather than succeed or fail.
open_points.question: What are the complete transitions from each waiting status to retry, continued waiting, success or failure?
options: service_unreachable retries on resume; unknown resolves to success, failure or approval-wait as A11 specifies
Both waits require an owner resolution
Every resolution must immediately produce a final conclusion
open_points.default_guess: Follow A11 and A14: resume retries service_unreachable; unknown applied becomes success or failure, and unknown not_applied becomes owner_approval waiting.

open_points.subject: ordering non-executable node conclusions
open_points.text: “The next node is the ready node with the smallest node_id” while skipped and upstream_failed nodes are concluded without executing, and A15 only orders records of nodes that “become non-executable together.”
open_points.question: When propagation makes some nodes skipped or upstream_failed while other nodes are ready, are all non-executable conclusions recorded first, are ready nodes executed first, or are both kinds processed in one node_id order; and what exactly makes conclusions occur “together”?
options: Close all newly non-executable nodes to a fixed point before executing another ready node
Choose the smallest node_id across ready and newly non-executable nodes
Execute ready nodes first and derive non-executable records only when no node is ready
open_points.default_guess: At each scheduling step, determine all newly non-executable nodes to a fixed point and record them in the stated node/map order before selecting the next ready node.

open_points.subject: resting run output shape
open_points.text: “A run that rests returns the outputs produced so far; the per-output reasons below are given only once it has ended” followed by “The run's answer names every flow output port with either its value or a reason.”
open_points.question: While a run is resting, are unproduced flow-output ports omitted, included with a nonfinal reason, or included with another placeholder?
options: Omit unproduced ports until the run ends
Include every port with not_produced while resting
Include every port with a distinct pending marker
open_points.default_guess: Return only produced output ports while resting; name every port with a value or final reason only after the run ends.

open_points.subject: mapped-list size failure across releases
open_points.text: A13 makes an oversized mapped list failure “derived from the elements' records and stored_value_bytes_max, the same way by every reader … after a restart,” while A20 allows a new release to change that ceiling and says recorded executions are never reinterpreted.
open_points.question: Which release's stored_value_bytes_max is used to derive an existing run's mapped-list conclusion after an upgrade?
options: The release ceiling pinned when the run started
The ceiling of the currently running release
Persist the derived size failure so it is no longer recomputed from a mutable release constant
open_points.default_guess: Use and persist the release ceiling applicable when the run started so recovery cannot reinterpret the run.
